uses: Mugwort has been used in Chinese, Hindu and European medicine, above all for women's complaints and the digestion; medieval herbalists called it the mother of herbs, and its name is linked to Artemis, protector of women in childbirth. In European folk practice a weak infusion was taken as a bitter for the stomach and appetite, and to bring on a late period. Before hops it flavored ale, and on the Continent it still seasons roast goose. In East Asia the dried leaf down is burned in moxibustion, a practice of warming points on the body with the smoldering herb. Its smell was thought to keep moths away.
energetics: Culpeper called mugwort binding, and hot and dry to the second degree
caution_pregnancy: Do not use mugwort in pregnancy. It is traditionally avoided then because it was used to bring on periods and to expel the afterbirth, large amounts may cause miscarriage, and NCCIH advises against any use in pregnancy. Safety while breastfeeding is largely unknown; avoid.
caution_medications: No interactions with medicines are documented. As a precaution, one review notes that mugwort may raise blood sugar and advises care in diabetes, so if you have diabetes or take diabetes medicines, ask your prescriber first. Talk to your provider before using it if you take any medicine.
caution_conditions: Do not use it if you are allergic to mugwort or any daisy-family (Asteraceae) plant. Mugwort pollen is a major cause of hay fever and allergic asthma, and swallowed pollen has caused anaphylaxis. People with mugwort pollen allergy can also react to some foods, among them celery, carrot, kiwi, peach and certain nuts and seeds. In skin tests, people with pollen allergies, mugwort included, were more often sensitive to kitchen herbs such as anise, caraway, thyme and mint. Large amounts may cause nausea, vomiting and nerve damage, and high blood pressure has been reported. The essential oil contains thujone and camphor, which EFSA flags as possibly harmful, though the research behind that is mostly on the concentrated oil. Not enough is known about safety in any form.
caution_duration: No source we read gives a safe length of use. Not enough is known about long-term safety; avoid regular or prolonged use.
caution_topical: Mugwort can cause allergic skin reactions such as dermatitis and hives, and contact dermatitis from handling the plant is reported. Not enough is known about safety on the skin.
garden_harvest_timing: Grieve gathered the leaves in August and dug the roots in autumn; Dioscorides advised cutting the flowering tops just before they open.
garden_water: Drought-tolerant; needs good drainage, as wet soil rots the roots
notes: A tall perennial, 2 to 4 feet, with deeply cut leaves dark green above and white and downy below. It spreads by underground runners, and any scrap of root can start a new plant, so it is an invasive weed in some areas; grow it in a pot or a contained bed. Grieve records the story that John the Baptist wore mugwort as a belt, and that a crown of it worn on St. John's Eve, or a sprig carried, guarded against evil, weariness and wild beasts. Culpeper places mugwort under Venus.
